articles.title: FBI questions donors as 2 Dan Sullivans compete in Alaska Senate race
articles.description: ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — The FBI on Friday began reaching out to donors of Dan J. Sullivan asking about potential deception, as federal authorities ramped up their investigation over the U.S. Senate candidate in Alaska who shares a name with the Republican incumbent. An Anchorage-based FBI agent visited a boat dealership in Petersburg, a small fishing community accessible only by air or water where the candidate lives. The agent left a business card for Charles Flint, who told The Associated Press he has known Dan J. Sullivan for years as a respected teacher and musician. The FBI visit came after federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over the candidate. The U.S. Department of Justice also pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion. Flint contributed $500 over the summer to what he considered a long-shot campaign, saying he knew Dan J. Sullivan would have expenses and respected him for “throwing his hat in the ring.” Flint said the FBI agent asked his son, who works at the dealership, whether Flint felt he had been “misled” about which candidate he was supporting. “I don’t feel like I’ve been misled at all,” Flint, who has been out of town, told the AP in a telephone interview, adding he had no intention of calling the agent but would “let him waste his time trying to track me down.” “I don’t think there’s any confusion,” he said, adding he intends to rank Democrat Mary Peltola first on his ballot, followed by Dan J. Sullivan. “Everybody knows who the incumbent is.” Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage the federal investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.” The developments come just days before Tuesday’s ranked choice general election in a potentially pivotal race in which Peltola, a former congresswoman, is challenging Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. At a campaign rally in Anchorage on Friday, Peltola again denied any involvement in any plan to place candidates on the ballot to detract from the incumbent senator. She said she was “deeply offended” by the allegations, which she called “garbage” and part of a “smear campaign” to suppress turnout on the eve of the election. “I know I can beat Dan Sullivan. I do not need any help winning this race,” she told a small group of campaign volunteers at an Anchorage aviation museum. ___ Mustian reported from New York. Associated Press reporter Becky Bohrer contributed reporting from Juneau, Alaska. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/fbi-visits-dan-j-sullivan-041854344.html

articles.title: Senate candidate leaves hometown as mystery swirls around high-stakes race: report
articles.description: An independent Senate candidate whose name closely resembles Alaska’s Republican incumbent left his hometown days before the election, adding another unanswered question to a closely watched race, according to a CBS News exclusive report. Daniel J. Sullivan departed Petersburg on Monday, multiple sources told the network. A former student saw him on a flight to Anchorage but did not know his ultimate destination. Back home, CBS found no visible evidence of active campaigning, including outside his home. Dozens of residents said they had seen or received no campaign materials since he announced his candidacy last spring. “I don't think it's a serious candidacy," fisherman Andrew Worhatch told CBS. "I haven't seen a platform.” Sullivan’s departure came two days before The New York Times reported that operatives linked to Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign recruited him. Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK) has called his similarly named opponent a “sham candidate.” Peltola and national Democrats deny any connection. She said she “knew nothing about” the second Sullivan and was “not interested in tricking voters.” The retired teacher has maintained that he genuinely wants to serve, according to CBS News. Supporter Keely Hankins defended him and said voters could distinguish the candidates. “Just read the paper. It's not that hard,” she told the network. The report does not establish why Sullivan traveled. A friend described him and his wife as “world travelers.” Meanwhile, Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation following the Times report, and the Trump DOJ expanded a criminal probe. Nobody has been charged, and a federal prosecutor refused to identify what, if any, crimes they were investigating. The DOJ is separately seeking to block certification if the incumbent loses because of “voter confusion.”

articles.title: Trump's canceled rallies now 'back on' in potential panic move: report
articles.description: President Donald Trump revived campaign rallies in Kansas and Iowa less than a day after canceling them, days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress. “Rallies are BACK ON!” read a statement that Fox News White House correspondent Jacqui Heinrich posted on X Friday morning, citing a source familiar with the plans. The Republican National Committee had called off both events Thursday, saying that “with Republicans in a strong position in Kansas and Iowa, previously planned in-person rallies in those states will no longer take place as scheduled,” Newsweek reported. Republicans claimed they had called off the rallies because they saw themselves in a strong position in both states, but by Friday morning both were back on. The new statement framed the reversal as a scheduling matter. “President Trump loves his supporters, and in addition to nearly 20 tele-rallies, he will hold back-to-back rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday,” the statement said. A White House official and a Republican official also confirmed the Sunday plans to CNN. The committee’s announcement Thursday had said that rather than appear in Kansas on Saturday and Iowa on Sunday, Trump would spend a “72-hour sprint” holding rallies by phone, which it said would let him reach voters nationwide, CBS News reported. “The rallies were rearranged for scheduling purposes to accommodate dozens of additional tele-rallies that were recently added to the President’s schedule,” Friday’s statement said. On Thursday, the tele-rallies were the reason for the cancellation. On Friday, the rallies were rearranged to make room for those same tele-rallies. Trump said Thursday that the Kansas race didn't need him, and he rejected a suggestion that his health caused the cancellation. “I’m not going to Kansas because he’s doing very well,” Trump said of Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS), according to Newsweek. But new polling showed Marshall trailing Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor, in a state Trump carried by 16 percentage points in 2024, Newsweek reported. The outlet said the canceled rally would have been Trump’s second in Kansas for Marshall this month. “I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas,” Trump said after a reporter asked whether he had canceled the trip because of his health, CBS News reported. “God didn’t make your vocal cords to do a rally every day,” Trump said in a hoarse voice Monday. He held 25 rallies in October, short of his goal of more than 30. Public polls suggest his visits have not had their intended effect, with Democrats unexpectedly competitive in Iowa, Kansas and other states. Vice President JD Vance also canceled a Friday press conference in Minnesota, CNBC reported. Republicans in Kansas and Iowa were split over whether they wanted Trump to come. Some top Republican operatives in both states quietly expressed relief at the canceled rallies.

articles.title: JD Vance town hall answer flagged by insiders as reason 'he's not our guy in 2028': MS NOW
articles.description: MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” panel criticized Vice President JD Vance’s response to a young woman at a town hall who said she couldn’t afford rent, groceries, student loans or gas, and The Atlantic’s Jonathan Lemire said moments like it have led people in Trump’s White House to question Vance as a 2028 pick. Joe Scarborough said the woman “pours her heart out” to the vice president, who responded by making a joke about a senator. Scarborough said Vance then blamed illegal immigrants for the housing crisis, which he said “is just not going to sail,” and called Vance “ill-equipped in so many ways for that position.” Former Sen. Claire McCaskill (D-MO) said the administration is “long on grift greed, but very short on empathy.” She disputed Vance’s substance, saying she asked how many immigrants are buying homes at the interest rates that average new homes at $415,000, and that Vance’s answer about ICE raids slowing construction was off base. Lemire said moments like that are ones “people in the Trump White House have flagged and said, like, maybe this isn’t our guy in ‘28.” He said Trump has also mused about the size of Vance’s rally crowds, and that voters say Republicans “don’t seem to care that we’re suffering.” Republicans he spoke with for a recent piece said broken promises on bringing down prices keep coming up. Lemire added that Vance was asked whether he’d promise not to be in any forever war, and dismissed the idea about Iran, though Lemire said he and others have reported a high likelihood of more U.S. strikes in the coming days or weeks.

articles.title: Pentagon reportedly tells NATO allies to tone down rhetoric about Russia
articles.description: By Antoni Slodkowski, Gram Slattery and Andrius Sytas Oct 30 (Reuters) - Pentagon officials have in recent weeks asked several NATO countries to tone down their rhetoric regarding the threat posed by Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials have undermined continental security, four people familiar with the matter said. Among the nations that have received messages urging them to keep public statements in check are Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. It was not clear if the messages, which were delivered in bilateral meetings, were conveyed to other European governments. The US requests come as the Trump administration restarts an effort to press for a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year. The latest push has blended incentives for Russia - including sanctions relief - with pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. Asked for comment, a Pentagon official said: "Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations." Among the comments that have drawn US officials' attention are suggestions by European leaders that Russia is cornered and resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slows to a crawl, one of the people said. Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of US troop levels in Europe, was one of the US officials delivering the message, the people said. Reuters could not determine what other officials were involved. None of the people, who include three European officials and a US official, suggested the advice was communicated in a confrontational manner. EUROPE SHOULD AVOID "POKING" RUSSIA The US messages reflect a debate within NATO regarding how to publicly address the threat of an increasingly assertive Russia. Some Western officials have argued that emphasizing the threat posed by Moscow could play into the hands of the Kremlin, which they say seeks to sow fear and undermine support for Ukraine. Others argue European governments must be transparent to show their electorates that sacrifice and resources are needed to keep Moscow at bay. That is especially true as Russia appears to accelerate a covert campaign of sabotage throughout the continent. Russia has denied that it is pursuing such a campaign. One of the people familiar told Reuters that Colby told a Baltic official recently that there should be no "poking" directed at the Russians. The person said Colby pointed to Europeans publicly suggesting that Russia was "cornered like a rat" as an example of unhelpful rhetoric. It was not clear what specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal referred to Putin as a "rat in a corner" in late September, suggesting the Russian leader was resorting to sabotage efforts in Europe as Russia had become increasingly bogged down in Ukraine. "We are helping you. The Americans are there," said a separate European official, describing the Pentagon's recent private messaging. "Just don't be loud. Don't make noise." In a separate recent meeting, the Pentagon urged an Estonian delegation to be "measured" in its communications, according to a person briefed on the encounter, though the person did not say Pentagon officials complained about any specific statement. The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment. MOSCOW TESTS EUROPE'S RESOLVE One of the European officials said that the Pentagon's advice, while cordial, was baffling, given that intelligence services in the Baltic states have in recent months consistently played down the probability of Russia testing NATO's mutual defense provisions. Other NATO intelligence services, by contrast, have publicly warned that Russia could dramatically ramp up its sabotage campaign in the near future. The Pentagon messages to NATO officials come at a fraught time for European security. Moscow has recently intensified its campaign of deniable attacks on NATO countries, Western intelligence officials have said. On Wednesday, German prosecutors said two Belarusians were arrested for allegedly planning to set fire to a building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg area. In September, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, allegations Moscow has denied. At the same time, US officials have been discussing potential business deals with Russia as part of the Trump administration's push for peace in Ukraine. Those efforts have drawn mixed reactions from European officials, many of whom are pushing for the Kremlin's continued economic isolation. Pentagon planners, meanwhile, are reviewing Washington's force posture in Europe, a process that could see a sharp drawdown in America's troop presence on the continent. US officials have said European NATO members need to assume more responsibility for their own defense, particularly as the US focuses on threats in the Middle East, Latin America and East Asia. (Reporting by Antoni Slodkowski in New York, Gram Slattery in Washington and Andrius Sytas in Vilnius; Additional reporting by Phil Stewart in Washington; Editing by Don Durfee and Alistair Bell) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/exclusive-pentagon-tells-europeans-cool-050400616.html

‘Ignorance towards immigration is horrible. It’s not British’: Skepta on his long-awaited return – and his anger at the racist right
articles.description: Thirty-three months after it was announced, the grime legend’s new album is coming out. He explains how skinheads, fatherhood and rap history came to bear on its socially conscious contents ‘I can’t be perfect,” Skepta says, pulling a black Arc’tyrex beanie down over a furrowed brow with both hands. “But I can be conscious.” The self-proclaimed king of grime has always been a serious person, wary of fools and time-wasters. Focus is important to him, perhaps because he’s often multitasking: balancing his music career, his fashion label Mains, film-making and acting (his debut short, Tribal Mark, came out in 2024), his Big Smoke festival and a house music project, Más Tiempo. He coordinates them all from the scruffy but functional studio in London’s West End where we meet. At one point, he picks up a Rubik’s Cube from the cluttered coffee table, and, over the course of five minutes of conversation, solves it. “This album has been winding me up,” he admits, referring to The Fork and Knife, which is out next week, 33 months after it was first announced. “But I think I’ve actually made something here that is what the people want from me.” Continue reading...
